title.en: The False Face's Bargain: The Contest of the Two Mountains
title.zh: 假臼者的交易：雙山較力

region.en: Grand River reserve, Ontario (related by David Boyle)
region.zh: 加拿大安大略格蘭德河保留地（大衛波義耳講述）

texts.period: Related by David Boyle on the Grand River, printed in W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore, gathered from the Six Nations of New York (1922), 'False Faces and Creation'

summary.en: After the making of the world and its people by Rawen Niyoh (Hawenneyu), he was one day walking through an open place, following the sun and examining the ground where the people were going to live, when his eye caught a strange, long-haired figure coming in the opposite direction, the face red and twisted, the mouth pulled up at the left corner. 'I am the real owner of this world. I was here before you.' To prove strength the False Face ordered one of two mountains to come nearer, and it moved close to them; Rawen Niyoh ordered the other mountain to approach, which it did, the two remaining so nearly together that they had hardly room to get out. Each was satisfied with this exhibition of power, and Rawen Niyoh said, 'I think it would not be well for you to be seen by the people who are coming to this place, because you are so ugly.' The False Face agreed to hide on condition that he should claim the new people as his grandchildren and be called Grandfather, 'I will help all I can to drive away sickness from among the new people, and I am able to protect them from storms by causing the winds to go up high into the sky.' 'They shall be your grandchildren and you their Grandfather. They must observe a dance - the False Face Dance - at the Long House forever. Now we make this bargain, which shall last as long as you and I, and the people and the world shall last.' In other stories the False Face fails to move the mountain.
summary.zh: 造物主哈威尼尤造好世界與人民之後，一日沿日而行，視察將有人煙的地土，迎面遇見一個奇異的長髮身影——紅面歪扭，嘴角向左上吊。「我才是這世界的真主，我比你先在。」為較力，假臼者命兩座山之一靠近，山果然移來；哈威尼尤命另一山前進，兩山幾乎相擠，二人險無容身之地。彼此服其神力；哈威尼尤說：「你如此醜陋，不宜讓將來的人們看見。」假臼者應允隱匿，條件是認新人類為孫、被稱作「祖父」，「我當盡力驅除人間疾病，又能使風暴高飛天空以護他們。」於是二人立約：人民行「假臼之舞」於長屋，直到永遠。另一些故事裡，假臼者移山失敗。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (Boyle informant); public domain. The False Face bargain is a living covenant of the medicine societies; no ritual details disclosed.

passages.text: After the making of the world and its people by Rawen Niyoh, he left it for a time, but when he returned he was one day walking through an open place, following the sun, overlooking his own work and examining the ground where the people were going to live, when his eye caught a strange, long-haired figure coming in the opposite direction. The face of this figure was red and twisted, the mouth being pulled up at the left corner. Rawen Niyoh (Hawenneyu) said to him: 'Where did you come from?' to which the False Face replied: 'I am the real owner of this world. I was here before you.' Rawen Niyoh said, 'I think I am the owner of this place, because I made it.' 'That may be quite true,' the False Face assented, 'but I have been here a long time, and I have a good claim to it, and I am stronger than you are.' 'Show me how you can prove this,' demanded Rawen Niyoh.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 12-13; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The False Face suggested that they should retire to a valley not far from two high mountains. The False Face ordered one of the mountains to come nearer, and it moved close to them. Rawen Niyoh was very much surprised at the result, on which he ordered the other mountain to approach, which it did - the two remaining so nearly together that Rawen Niyoh and the False Face had hardly room to get out. Each was satisfied with this exhibition of power on the part of the other, and Rawen Niyoh said, 'I think it would not be well for you to be seen by the people who are coming to this place, because you are so ugly, for every one would follow you to look at you.' Ak-on-wa-rah (the False Face) agreed to this on condition that he should be allowed to claim the new people as his grandchildren, and they were to call him Grandfather. 'I will help all I can,' said he, 'to drive away sickness from among the new people, and I am able to protect them from storms by causing the winds to go up high into the sky.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 13-14; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Rawen Niyoh replied, 'I am sure you have much power to help the people, and you must keep this power as long as they live. We will make a bargain. They shall be your grandchildren and you their Grandfather. They must observe a dance - the False Face Dance - at the Long House forever. Now we make this bargain, which shall last as long as you and I, and the people and the world shall last.' Akonwarah replied, 'It is well.' In other stories the False Face fails to move the mountain.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 14; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Terrible Skeleton of the Adirondack Cabin
title.zh: 阿迪朗達克木屋中的可怕骸骨

region.en: Hunting camp in the Adirondacks, from the Onondaga reservation
region.zh: 奧農達加獵隊在阿迪朗達克的營屋

texts.period: Told by Albert Cusick (Sa-go-na-qua-de), published 1888; reprinted by Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'The Terrible Skeleton'

summary.en: An Onondaga hunting party once went off with an old man, his daughter and her husband, and their little boy; the boy accidentally went the other way with his uncle. Late in the day the three found an empty cabin in a clearing and resolved to stay the night. When the fire became low and it grew dark, the young people were aroused by a sound like a dog gnawing a bone - it was a terrible skeleton, feeding on the old man. The wife slipped away to 'the spring,' the husband followed a little later, and as the fire went down the skeleton found both gone and started in chase. That night the Onondagas had a great dance: the fugitives heard the drum far away, turn-turn, turn-turn, and shouted; their friends heard the distress-hallo and came with all their arms, and the skeleton fled. A council sent the warriors to the dreadful spot: in the loft was a bark coffin with the skeleton of a man left unburied by his friends. Fuel was gathered and fire applied; the fire grew hot, the cabin fell in, and out of the flames rushed a fox with red and fiery eyes, dashed through the ranks and disappeared in the forest. The dead hunter was seen no more. 'But what had the little boy to do with all this?' 'O, that is to show it was well he went the other way.'
summary.zh: 奧農達加獵隊遠行，同行的有老人、其女與女婿，還有小男孩——男孩卻誤隨舅父走了另一條路。三人在空曠地的空屋過夜。火弱天黑之際，年輕夫婦聽見如犬啃骨的聲響——原來是一具可怕骸骨，正在啃食老人。妻子藉口「口渴去泉邊」先溜，丈夫稍後藉口尋妻而逃；火滅之後骸骨見二人皆走，隨後狂追。當夜奧農達加正舉行大舞：逃者遠聞鼓聲「轉—轉、轉—轉」，邊跑邊喊；族人聞救命呼聲持械而至，骸骨遁走。戰士們奉議前往：閣樓上有具樹皮棺，內是一具被族人棄而不葬的骸骨。眾人堆柴縱火；火旺屋塌，一隻紅眼的火狐自焰中竄出，穿陣而逃。死者從此不再現形。「那小男孩與這事有何相干？」「噢，那正是要說明：他走另一條路，走對了。」

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (Albert Cusick informant); public domain. Cusick's grandfather David Cusick briefly related the same tale - a burial-custom aition.

passages.text: In old times the Onondagas lived on a much larger reservation than now - a great land - but they made hunting parties to the Adirondacks. A party once went off in which were an old man, his daughter and her husband, and their little boy. They went one day and camped, and another day and camped, and then separated... late in the day found an empty cabin in a clearing... they resolved to stay for the night. They gathered plenty of fuel, stripping long pieces from the shag-bark hickory, built a fine fire, spread their deerskins on the rude bedsteads, and then went to sleep - the old man on one side, and the man and his wife on the other.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 13-14; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: When the fire became low and it grew dark in the cabin, the young people were aroused by a sound like a dog gnawing a bone. They stirred about and the noise ceased, but was followed by something like rattling bones overhead. They arose and put on more fuel, and were going back to bed when they saw a dark stream from the other couch. It was blood and the old man was dead. His clothes were torn open and his ribs broken and gnawed. They covered him and lay down again. The same thing happened the second time, and this time they saw it was a terrible skeleton, feeding on the dead man. They were frightened and in whispers devised a plan of escape. They made a greater fire, and the wife said to her husband, 'I am so thirsty; I must go to the spring and have a long drink.' She went quietly out, but a little way off ran with all her might toward her own country. When her husband thought she had a good start he made a very big fire, to last a great while, and then he said, 'What has become of my wife? I am afraid she is drowned in the spring. I must go and see.' So he went out, and a little way off he, too, ran with all his might.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 14; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: By and by the fire went down, the skeleton came again, and when he found both were gone he started in chase. Soon they heard him howling terribly behind them and ran the faster for this. It happened that night that the Onondagas had a great dance and it now drew near morning. The fugitives heard the drum far away, turn-turn, turn-turn, and ran faster and shouted, but the skeleton did the same... Their friends heard the distress-hallo and came with all their arms. The skeleton fled. The fugitives fainted and did not regain their senses for four hours.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 14-15; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: A council was held and the warriors started for the dreadful spot. They found the hut and a few traces of the old man. In the loft were some scattered articles and a bark coffin. In this was the skeleton of a man left unburied by his friends. It was determined to destroy everything. Fuel was gathered and fire applied. The warriors stood around with bended bows and raised hatchets. The fire grew hot, the cabin fell in, and out of the flames rushed a fox with red and fiery eyes, dashed through the ranks and disappeared in the forest. The dead hunter was seen no more. 'But what had the little boy to do with all this?' 'O, that is to show it was well he went the other way.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 15; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Hunter Whose Friend Married the Big Serpent
title.zh: 與巨蛇成婚的朋友：雷族的誘殺

region.en: Group of lakes at Tully, Onondaga country (perhaps Crooked Lake and Round Lake)
region.zh: 奧農達加塔利湖群（或即克湖與圓湖）

texts.period: Told at Onondaga Castle by an old Oneida, related by Albert Cusick (published 1888; Beauchamp 1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), the serpent-wife tale told by Sa-go-na-qua-de

summary.en: Two young men, close friends, hunt far from home; the handsome one returns gameless day after day until his friend follows him: he plunges into the lakes, swims across 'like a snake,' and confesses he is going to be married - to the big serpent in the lake - and must leave his friend alone, though he may call him to the shore with fresh Indian tobacco and clean clay pipes laid on new bark, saying to the lake, 'I want to see my friend.' A youth dressed in white with white feathers on his head comes to the lonely hunter: 'My chief has sent me to invite you to our council' - eight chiefs in white feathers, whose plan is to destroy the serpent and his silver-shining wife, and who will come 'in the form of a cloud; on the lake, not in the sky.' The hunter lays the offering, calls his friend, is asked to lead the pair away from the lake into the woods - then runs; a great cloud comes at once over everything, and terrible thunder and lightning follow where they had sat, with rain everywhere. A big and a little serpent lie dead on the ground - the serpent woman and his friend. The eight chiefs cut up both serpents, making eight equal bundles, each chief carrying one, and go off in Indian file, seeming to step higher and higher until they went up to the sky, in a great thunder storm - for the chiefs were the Thunderers. The sorrowing hunter is adopted by his friend's mother and has two mothers.
summary.zh: 兩位親密的朋友遠行打獵；俊美者日日空手而歸。朋友跟蹤他：他竄入湖中「如蛇般」游過，坦白說他將成婚——娶湖中的大蛇為妻——並教朋友日後以新樹皮墊著新鮮菸草與潔淨陶管置於岸邊，對湖說「我想見我的朋友」。一日一位白衣白羽的青年來到孤獨的獵人門前：「我的首領派我來請你入議。」八位白羽酋長的計策是誅殺蛇夫婦；他們將「化為一片雲——在湖面上，而非天上」。獵人如言設供、喚友，並邀蛇夫婦離湖入林——隨後脫身而逃；烏雲立時罩天，雷電暴雨盡落二人坐處。湖畔躺著一大一小兩條死蛇——蛇妻與他的朋友。八位酋長把蛇切成八份，各背一份，列隊而去，步履漸高，升天而去——雷聲大作，因為他們就是雷族。悲傷的獵人被朋友的母親收養，從而有兩位母親。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922; public domain. Beauchamp notes the tale is unique though with features peculiar to thunder-god stories.

passages.text: A long time ago, in an Indian settlement, were two wigwams not far apart, and in these lived two squaws who were very good friends. They had two children of about the same age, who played together... They were now young men and good hunters. One of them, being handsome and kind, was very much liked by the women and some of the maidens would have married him, but he refused all offers. At last his friend talked with him, and told him he had better marry, or something might happen for which he would be sorry. This troubled him, and he said he would soon choose a wife, but first they would have a long hunt together. They got ready for this, telling their mothers they were going away on a great hunt, far from their village, and might be gone many days. So their mothers took some corn and roasted it, and then pounded this into meal in their wooden mortars. The young men filled their sacks, took their bows, and went to their hunting ground.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 15-16; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: After this they hunted every day, and one was lucky and brought home a great deal of game, but the one whom the girls liked came home without any, and said very little. Every morning they went to hunt in opposite directions, and one day his friend thought he would follow him and see what he did. He soon saw him running very fast through the woods and hurried after him, calling to him to stop, but he did not. They ran till they came to a lake, and the first one plunged into the water and swam across, while his friend went around the shore... As the swimmer entered the other jumped out and caught him, asking what was the matter and why he acted so strangely. At first the young man could say nothing and seemed to know nothing, but soon came to his senses. He told his friend that he was going to be married and must leave him all alone, for he could not go back to his home. If he wished to see him at any time, he might come to the lake, bringing fresh Indian tobacco and clean clay pipes. These things he must lay on bark just from the tree, and must then say to the lake, 'I want to see my friend.' So he went off another way and married the big serpent in the lake.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 16-17; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: When he turned around a young man stood in the doorway, dressed in white and with white feathers on his head. The visitor said, 'You seem to be in trouble, but for all that you are the only one that can help us. My chief has sent me to invite you to our council.' Then he gave him wampum, to show that he brought a true message... Going in, he saw eight chiefs sitting quietly on the ground. All had white feathers on their heads, but the principal chief had larger feathers than the rest... 'Your friend has married the big serpent in the lake, whom we must kill... When your friend comes you must ask to see his wife. She will want to know if the sky is clear. When she comes you must take them a little way from the lake and talk to them there. The chiefs will come in the form of a cloud; on the lake, not in the sky.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 17-18; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then the hunter remembered the chief's words, and at last saw something like a cloud a great way off, moving upon the water and not through the sky. Then he asked them to go into the woods, where the sun was not so hot, and there talk with him. When they did this he said he must step aside, and then he ran away, as the chiefs had told him. As he ran, a great cloud came at once over everything, and terrible thunder and lightning followed where they had sat, with rain everywhere. At last all was quiet again and the hunter went back to the lake, where a big and a little serpent lay dead on the ground. They were the serpent woman and his friend. The eight chiefs were there, too, and had a dance, rejoicing over their dead enemy. When this was over they cut up both serpents, making eight equal bundles of them. Each chief put one on his back and then they were ready to go. All thanked the young man for what he had done, and told him he would always be lucky... Then they went off through the woods in Indian file, and as he looked they seemed to step higher and higher, until they went up to the sky. Then there was a great thunder storm, for the chiefs were the Thunderers. The hunter went back to his wigwam, but it was quiet and lonesome and he was sad... she was very sorry for the death of the son whom she had loved, but adopted him in his place, and so the young man had two mothers.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 18-19; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: O-kwen-cha, Red Paint: The Boy Who Beat the Drum and Freed His Uncles
title.zh: 紅漆兒奧克文查：擊鼓喚舅的男孩

region.en: Old Ka-no-sa hon-we in the Onondaga woods, and the lands to the west
region.zh: 奧農達加林中的老屋，及其以西之地

texts.period: Told by Albert Cusick, from Bill Lije (Soo-noo-weh), a famous storyteller (Beauchamp 1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'O-kwen-cha, or Red Paint'

summary.en: A knee-high boy, O-kwen-cha or Red Paint, lives with his old grandmother Cho-noo-kwa-a-nah (Uncombed Coarse Hair) in an old moss-roofed cabin hung with weapons and dried meat, forbidden the Indian drum. At last he beats it, singing his war song 'Ha-wa-sa-say!' - and out from under the four beds come his uncles, dancing the war dance, their dancing heard throughout the world; when the drum is hung up they are no more to be seen. The drum-and-dancing is heard by all the people with magic powers, and a very tall man appears: 'Three days from to-day you are to appear at my place, and be ready for a grand wrestling match. We are to bet for our heads.' Sus-ten-ha-nah, He Large Stone, lives on human flesh and never was beat in wrestling. Red Paint, now very powerful in magic, comes through the stone crying 'Give me the chance, grandmother!'; torn in two pieces and thrown aside, he comes again - throws Large Stone three times, cuts off his head, and when the head flies up the third time they draw the body onto the flat stone, so that head and stone both burst into a thousand pieces scattered over the world - that is why stones lie about everywhere - and the brains became snails, that is why they are found everywhere. Gathering the bones of the slain, he pushes a great hickory: 'Take care! This tree will fall over you' - the bones come to life and run, some with short backs, some big heads on little bodies; he exchanges parts until men look like men and bears and deer as they should, and travels west to free the rest of his uncles, even breathing his fourth uncle back to life from his own skin, and finally smoothing his aged grandmother's wrinkles with a little stick until she seems a handsome young woman again.
summary.zh: 膝高的男孩奧克文查（紅漆）與老祖母「亂髮婆婆」住在苔頂老屋，被禁止碰壁上的印第安鼓。他終於擊鼓唱起戰歌「哈瓦薩塞！」——四張床下走出他的舅舅們，跳起戰舞，舞聲傳遍世界；鼓一掛回，舅舅們便不見了。鼓聲與舞聲傳到所有具法力者耳中，一位高得進不了屋的巨人現身：「三天後你到我處，賭頭摔跤。」大石人蘇斯滕哈納以人肉為食、摔跤從未落敗。此時的紅漆已具大法：他穿石而出喊「讓我來，祖母！」被撕成兩半拋開，又再現身——三次摔倒大石人，割下其頭；頭第三次飛天時，他們把屍身拖上平石，頭與石同時迸作千片散佈世界——石頭遍地皆是之由——腦髓化為蝸牛，故蝸牛遍佈。他集攏被害者的骸骨，推倒大核桃樹喊「小心！樹要倒了」——骸骨復活奔逃，短背長腿、頭身錯配；他一一換正，再西行解放其餘舅舅，甚至對著人皮吹氣使第四位舅舅復活，最後以小杖撫平祖母的皺紋，使她重現少婦容顏。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922; public domain. Cusick thought it a genuine old Onondaga story; the bones-and-falling-tree motif recurs in early Iroquois legends and in a 1921 Caddo variant.

passages.text: There was once, a long time ago, a little boy named O-kwen-cha or Red Paint, who lived with his old grandmother in an old Ka-no-sa hon-we, or old-fashioned house, which had no windows and but one doorway... O-kwen-cha's grandmother did all the work, brought all the wood and killed all the game... She went away every day but always told him, when about to leave, that he must not touch the drum that hung upon the wall. One day, getting tired with his games, he thought he would amuse himself with something new. So he got upon the bed and reached the drum. Then he began to drum and to chant his war song: 'Ha-wa-sa-say! Ha-wa-sa-say!' etc. Then came his uncles from under the four beds, dancing the war dance. When they did this their dancing was heard throughout the world.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 20-21; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: So the world and its people, and the bad men with magic powers (orenda), heard the beating of the drum and the dancing, and the running of the old woman. Then the people said, 'He, Ha!... So Cho-noo-kwa-a-nah (Uncombed Coarse Hair), is in trouble again. We will soon know which of the men with magic powers will try to take her life.' On the third day he made his uncles dance again, and the world heard the drum and dancing, and the running of Cho-noo-kwa-a-na. This time she had not been very far, so she caught him with the drum still in his hands. She had said hardly a word when a very tall man appeared... 'Three days from to-day you are to appear at my place, and be ready for a grand wrestling match. We are to bet for our heads. If I throw you three times I will cut your head off, and if you throw me three times you may cut my head off and save your life.' His name was Sus-ten-ha-nah, or 'He Large Stone,' for he lived on a very large flat stone. He lived on human flesh, and never was beat in wrestling. He cut off the heads of all whom he threw and ate their flesh.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 21-23; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Cho-noo-kwa-a-nah got up on the flat stone. Hardly had she done this when Large Stone seized her by the neck and was going to throw her on the stone. Just then he heard some one calling to him, 'Here, here! that is not the way to wrestle. Here, here! give me the chance, grandmother!'... when O-kwen-cha appeared, coming through the stone... Red Paint, small as he was, was now very powerful in magic. 'Ho, ho,' said Large Stone, 'So you want to wrestle with me, do you? What do you amount to?' said he, at the same time clutching him by the legs. He tore his body in two pieces and threw them aside. Then he went at Coarse Hair again, but up came O-kwen-cha again, crying, 'Give me the chance, grandmother!' So she let him try again. He threw Large Stone three times... As soon as this was done the head flew high up in the air... The third time, when the head flew up, the boy said to his grandmother, 'Let us draw the body to one side,' and they laid it on the flat stone. When the head came down it struck on the stone, and that flew into a thousand pieces, which were scattered all over the world. That is why we have stones lying about everywhere. The head also broke into a thousand pieces, which flew all over the earth, and the brains became snails and that is why they are found everywhere.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 23-24; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then he told her to go home alone. When she had gone, he gathered all the bones that lay there, of those whom Sus-ten-ha-nah had killed, and put them all together in a row - all that he could find. Then he went to a great hickory tree which stood there, and called out, 'Euch! Euch!' or 'Take care! take care! This tree will fall over you; you had better get out of the way!' He pushed hard on the tree, and the big tree fell, and the bones came to life and began to run away. Some had short backs, and some short legs, and some had big heads on little bodies, or little heads on big bodies; while some had the heads of bears, and others of deer or wolves, for the right bones had not always come together. When Red Paint saw how oddly they looked, he made them exchange heads and bodies... so that the men looked like men, and the bears and deer as bears and deer should. When Red Paint was going homeward by himself... Then he began to breathe in the mouth of the skin, and the last of his four uncles came to life again. When they got inside, Red Paint found his grandmother had become very old... When he saw her look so old, Red Paint said, 'I will make a young woman out of my grandmother yet.' Then he took a little stick and stuck it in the back of her ear, under the loose skin, and twisted it till all the wrinkles were straightened out, and her face became smooth again.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 24-30; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Speaking Pine: The Warrior Chief Who Became the Forest Guide
title.zh: 會說話的松：化身林中嚮導的戰酋

region.en: The pine whose top branches point east and west

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), the Speech of the Tall Pine

summary.en: And the Tall Pine said: 'Once I walked the earth a warrior chief, and in my quiver was death. My arrows cried shrill and strong on their journeys to kill. They were feathered for blood... I was strong and bold, and hated my foe. I was stealthy, and haughty, and strode like the stag on my path... When I hunted my foe my footfall was still as the feather that drops from the flying bird, and the earth knew no sign of the moccasin track. Like a wolf I scented the blood of my foe and his heart that dripped sweet as the sunrise dew, and I followed him swift in my hungry hunt... I knew no pain of the torture brand, I sang to its flame my forefather's song as I welcomed the fire and red death with scorn... My spirit was strong, and could not die. It led my blood on its wasting way and nourished its flow as my veins throbbed fast for the seeding roots of my branches that boast... And my spirit said when it builded me: I will make you tall, and forever the tower and guide of your forest kin. On your topmost reach I will hang the horns that as warrior you wore, and I will set them high... I am the Pine! the guide of my forest kin! I rock the sunlights to drowse in my arms as the winds waft my fragrance afar. In my silence the night shadows dream of the day as I tower strong and high and reach to the sky!'
summary.zh: 高松開言：「我曾是行於大地的戰爭酋長，箭囊中滿是死亡。我的箭羽蘸血、銳鳴奪命……我強悍高傲，如牡鹿闊步征途。追獵仇敵時，我足音輕如飛鳥落羽，大地不見鹿皮鞋的蹤跡。我如狼嗅得仇敵的血與他那滴如朝露般甘美的心，餓狩疾追……我不知火刑之痛，面向烈焰唱起先人的歌，傲然迎向火與紅色的死亡……我的靈強健不死。它領我的血流涓涓不止，滋養我枝椏的根……我的靈築我時說：我要使你高聳，永為林中親族的塔與嚮導；我要在你最高處懸上你為戰士時所戴的角徽……我是松！林中親族的嚮導！我在臂彎裡搖著日光入夢，風把我的芳香送遠。靜夜裡，夜影在我高聳擎天的身影下夢見白晝！」

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. First-person continuation of the Tall Pine myth.

passages.text: And the Tall Pine said: 'Once I walked the earth a warrior chief, and in my quiver was death. My arrows cried shrill and strong on their journeys to kill. They were feathered for blood. They were plunged with the poison that slays. They were winged to the winds that found the way in their swift death flight, and they never came back to me! I was strong and bold, and hated my foe. I was stealthy, and haughty, and strode like the stag on my path. To my listening ear the death moan was soft as the call of the doe. When I hunted my foe my footfall was still as the feather that drops from the flying bird, and the earth knew no sign of the moccasin track. Like a wolf I scented the blood of my foe and his heart that dripped sweet as the sunrise dew, and I followed him swift in my hungry hunt.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 55; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: 'I knew no pain of the torture brand, I sang to its flame my forefather's song as I welcomed the fire and red death with scorn, and the sun glared glad as it looked down on me... My spirit was strong, and could not die. It led my blood on its wasting way and nourished its flow as my veins throbbed fast for the seeding roots of my branches that boast. And my spirit said when it builded me: I will make you tall, and forever the tower and guide of your forest kin. On your topmost reach I will hang the horns that as warrior you wore, and I will set them high. When the sun sleeps and clouds blanket low, the kin of your forest will know where the east trail winds and the west trail guides.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 55-56; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And the Speaking Pine said: 'My spirit has builded, and I watch the sky. When strong tempests battle, I war with their rage as, in their moaning, voices return from my dead; and, as of old, I toss them back to the killing winds. When the soughing breeze passes my strong watchtower, a life stirs in me that is gentle and kind as the mother bird brooding her young, and I open my arms wide to the singing wind that tunes me to dreams. Thus forever I watch as my horns lift to the touch of the morning sun and flush to its west fire glow. I am the Pine! the guide of my forest kin! I rock the sunlights to drowse in my arms as the winds waft my fragrance afar. In my silence the night shadows dream of the day as I tower strong and high and reach to the sky!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 56; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Ga-do-waas and His Star Belt: The Milky Way

region.en: The Milky Way spanning the top sky

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ga-do-waas, his Star Belt, the Milky Way'

summary.en: Ga-do-waas dwells in the top sky, and with his four eyes watches every corner of the earth. At one time Ga-do-waas was an earth dweller and a hunter, but because of his presuming to celestial power and destroying all the game, he was transferred to the heavens, and watches the gate through which each soul passes to immortality. When Ga-do-waas assumed his duty as soul watcher, he removed his hunting belt, which possessed the charm of enticing game, and decorating it with stars, cast it into space, where it spans the entire heavens and illuminates each path to which he guides a soul. So luminous is this path that its blended light reaches down to the earth and divides its rays, stationing one at each lodge where a human is dying, that the departing soul may not lose its way as it leaves the dead. No human has seen these rays, they are visible only to the soul. The south wind accompanies the soul till it reaches the gate where Ga-do-waas watches, and as it passes the portal of this journey place, he reaches into space and grasps a star which he fastens in the belt, thereby to guide the soul on its journey. When the soul has crossed the entire heavens, Ga-do-waas removes the star from his belt, and returns it to its appointed place in space. Though each soul may pass through various transmigrations before it departs from its lower existence, it can not enter the Happy Hunting Ground till it has crossed the star belt of Ga-do-waas - therefore the Milky Way, to the Indian, is a procession of stars, each guiding a soul.
summary.zh: 加多瓦斯居於天頂，以四目環視大地的每個角落。他原是地上的獵人，因僭越天權、獵絕百獸，被移上天界，看守眾魂通往不朽的門戶。就任魂之守望者時，他解下那條能引誘獵物的獵帶，綴滿星辰擲入太空——星帶橫跨全天，照亮他引魂而行的每一條路。那路光輝燦然，光達地面，分出一縷縷光線，立於每一座有垂死之人的屋前，使離體之魂不致迷途。凡人看不見這些光，唯魂可見。南風伴魂直到守望之門；魂過門檻時，加多瓦斯伸手入太空摘下一顆星繫於帶上，為魂引路。魂渡盡諸天，他便把星取下歸位。魂雖經種種轉生，卻必先渡過加多瓦斯的星帶方能入極樂獵場——故在印第安人眼中，銀河是一列引魂的星。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. Parker footnotes Handsome Lake's own road-of-souls vision - most tracks in the Milky Way were those of children.

At one time, Ga-do-waas was an earth dweller and a hunter, but because of his presuming to celestial power and destroying all the game, he was transferred to the heavens, and watches the gate through which each soul passes to immortality.

So luminous is this path that its blended light reaches down to the earth and divides its rays, stationing one at each lodge where a human is dying, that the departing soul may not lose its way as it leaves the dead. No human has seen these rays, they are visible only to the soul. The south wind accompanies the soul till it reaches the gate where Ga-do-waas watches, and as it passes the portal of this journey place, he reaches into space and grasps a star which he fastens in the belt, thereby to guide the soul on its journey.

If there is a confusion in this procession, it is because some soul is disturbed and out of the path; but the star, which never loses its way, will search for it and return it to its course.

title.en: Nya-gwa-ih, the Celestial Bear: The Three Brothers and the Dog Ji-yeh
title.zh: 天熊尼亞瓜伊：三兄弟與獵犬吉耶

region.en: Ursa Major in the north sky (symbolic pin at the flat earth's northern edge)
region.zh: 北天的大熊星座（象徵性定位於大地北緣）

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Nya-gwa-ih, the Celestial Bear'

summary.en: The Iroquois had been disturbed by the ravages of an enormous bear which was devouring their winter game; baffling all their plans for its death, the nya-gwa-ih continued his ravage of plunder. One night each of three brothers dreamed he had found the bear, and they silently left the village on their secret hunt, accompanied by their faithful dog Ji-yeh, whose keen nose ridged the snow down to the trail. One night the terrified people hid from its roaring voice, and a deep snowfall always followed these visitations. Bundling the fire brush on the shoulders of one brother, to their belts they tied their bags of o-na-oh, the roasted corn flour, and set out on the chase: at night they slept not, during the day they rested not, for the elusive shadow of the rapid running bear could be seen on the snow hills as they ran to the north sky. The freezing winds pursued them, the ice weighted down their moccasins, and the pitiless snows drifted near to the skies; but impelled by their dream, the intrepid hunters faltered not until they had reached the end of the flat earth where it edges close to the north sky. Climbing higher and higher and farther away from the earth, they again saw the bear, who was now slow in its path, yet mighty as it pushed the white clouds before it, weaving an invisible net which it cast over the skies and crawled under to rest. Rejoicing to find him sleeping - 'We will not lose it now, and will carry it back to our people' - the listening bear slowly opened its sleepy eyes, and rising in its giant height, lifted the net with its huge paws and, dragging the hunters under it, drove them far away to roam the broad skies forever! And the hunters and their faithful dog, Ji-yeh, unknowing their imprisonment under the invisible net, are ceaselessly following the snow bear, who ever eludes them. In Ursa Major the Iroquois find these three hunters, one with the brush upon his back, and close following they trace the faithful dog, Ji-yeh.
summary.zh: 一頭巨熊年年掠食獵物，攪得易洛魁人不得安生；諸般獵策皆敗，尼亞瓜伊仍肆行劫掠。一夜，三兄弟同夢見熊，翌晨悄然出村密獵，攜忠犬吉耶——牠的靈鼻能把雪犁到蹤跡。他們把引火柴捆上肩、腰繫炒玉米粉的乾糧袋，晝夜不休地追：黑影在雪丘上閃現，引他們一路奔向北天。寒風窮追、冰凌墜靴、飛雪彌天，三人仍不放緩，直至大地的平緣貼近北天之處。他們攀得愈來愈高，再看見那熊——步子已慢，卻推著白雲前行，織出一張看不見的網罩住天穹，鑽入網下歇息。見牠酣睡，獵人們歡呼「這回跑不掉了，要把它抬回村去」——巨熊緩緩睜開惺忪睡眼，巨掌掀網，把獵人們拖入網下，驅向廣漠的天空永世流浪！三兄弟與忠犬吉耶不知自己已被困於無形之網下，只是不停地追逐那永遠逃脫的雪熊。在北斗之中，易洛魁人認得出這三個獵人——一個背上還捆著柴——以及緊隨其後的忠犬吉耶。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. Parker's long note argues the bear-constellation myth is Precolumbian: the bear's blood and oil spill to redden the leaves, the bear revives before the fire is kindled, and the pursuit goes on again.

passages.text: The Iroquois had been disturbed by the ravages of an enormous bear which was devouring their winter game. Numbers of the hunters had banded together and plodded through all the forests in search of it, but to no avail. At times it would near for a moment but to distance their arrows in a most mysterious way, and the blinding snow would fall fast and thick as if to cover its track. In the darkness it frequently prowled near the villages, when the terrified people would hide from its roaring voice, and a deep snowfall always followed these visitations; and baffling all their plans for its death, the nya-gwa-ih continued his ravage of plunder.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 57-58; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The winter was fierce in its cold blasts, and the snows had drifted mountains high in the forest; the trails were lost; the deer were vanishing, and their haunts were strewn with their bones which the nya-gwa-ih had left behind him, when one night each of three brothers dreamed he had found the bear, and deeply impressed by the remarkable coincidence on the following morning they silently left the village and started on their secret hunt, accompanied by their faithful dog, Ji-yeh, whose keen nose ridged the snow down to the trail... Having thus determined, they bundled the fire brush on the shoulders of one of the brothers, and to their belts tied their strong bags of o-na-oh, the roasted corn flour which would sustain them while they were running, and again set out on the chase.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 58; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: At night they slept not; during the day they rested not; for the elusive shadow of the rapid running bear could be seen on the snow hills as they ran to the north sky. As if avenging, the freezing winds pursued them, the ice weighted down their moccasins, and the pitiless snows drifted near to the skies; but impelled by their dream, the intrepid hunters faltered not until they had reached the end of the flat earth where it edges close to the north sky... Yet the tireless hunters would not rest, but climbed higher and higher and farther away from the earth, when again they saw the bear, who was now slow in its path, yet mighty as it pushed the white clouds before it, weaving an invisible net which it cast over the skies and crawled under to rest.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 58-59; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Astray in the strange place, the untiring hunters, who knew not fatigue nor hunger, rejoiced when they came near the bear to find him sleeping. 'We will not lose it now, and will carry it back to our people,' was their victorious cry. The listening bear slowly opened its sleepy eyes, and rising in its giant height, lifted the net with its huge paws and, dragging the hunters under it, drove them far away to roam the broad skies forever! And the hunters and their faithful dog, Ji-yeh, unknowing their imprisonment under the invisible net, are ceaselessly following the snow bear, who ever eludes them. In Ursa Major, the Iroquois find these three hunters, one with the brush upon his back, and close following they trace the faithful dog, Ji-yeh.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 59; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: So-son-do-wah and the Sky Elk: The Sentinel of Dawn
title.zh: 索翁多瓦與天麋：黎明的哨衛

region.en: Earth forest and the lodge of Dawn in the east sky
region.zh: 大地森林與東天黎明女神的居所

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'O-je-a-neh-doh, the Sky Elk'

summary.en: He was a mighty hunter, the So-son-do-wah! In the morning light the forest where O-je-a-neh-doh, the Sky Elk, stood silent as a shadow held a strange shape: the elk had wandered far in the earth forest all the night - the sun does not shine on the elk fields of the sky, so far above it, whence O-je-a-neh-doh had lingered too long to return. By the law of his religion the hunter must give all game a chance for its life: he shook a small sapling as a warning, and the elk sped through the tangled ways as So-son-do-wah sent his swift arrows after him - arrows which struck only to fall blunt to the ground. Hour after hour the elk ran on, up the rise and down the low places, across streams, until it leaped up the white-headed hills of the sky; the hunter caught on the wing of a swift bird of the night which soared to the farthermost part of the sky - yet the Sky Elk, more fleet in his own free fields, ever eluded the dumb arrows, until day feathered the sky, when the night bird shook So-son-do-wah back to the earth. But Dawn, pitying the hunter, rescued him as he was falling, and carrying him to her lodge in the east sky, created him her sentinel to guard its door. His heart yearned back to the earth for a maiden by the river; borrowing the body of a bluebird he sang 'ji-nya-ah' on her shoulder, of a blackbird he whistled 'ga-go-ji' close to her lips - 'It is I!' So-son-do-wah plaintively sighed from the heart of the bird, but the maiden heard not - and at last from a giant night hawk he swooped down and, lifting her to its broad wings, bore her to the skies. Dawn reproved him, transformed the maiden into a star, and as punishment bound his arms, placing the new star on his forehead and a flaming torch in her hand, which will consume him should he attempt to release himself. And thus he remains So-son-do-wah, the human hunter, who yet yearns for the star which has never known him.
summary.zh: 索翁多瓦是何等偉大的獵人！晨光裡，林間立著一個影一般的怪物——天麋奧杰內多，牠在地上的森林中迷途整夜：天上麋場無日光，牠流連太久，回不去了。獵人依其信仰之律，須先警獵物逃生：他搖動小樹作警，天麋竄逃，獵箭連發，箭箭觸身即鈍然落地。一人一獸逐過丘壑溪流，直至天麋躍上白頭的天丘；獵人攀上一隻夜鳥之翼直上遠天——天麋在自家原野疾如閃電，箭箭落空；天色泛紅時，夜鳥把獵人抖落塵寰。黎明女神憐其墜落，救起他，攜往東天居所，立他為守門的哨衛。獵人的心卻繫著河邊的少女：他借藍鶇之身停在她的肩頭唱「吉尼亞」；借黑鳥之身貼近她的唇邊吹「加戈吉」——「是我呀！」他在鳥心中悲嘆，少女卻聽不見。最後他借巨夜鷹之軀俯衝而下，展翅將她攜上天空。黎明女神斥其擅離職守，把少女化為星辰，並縛其雙臂以為懲罰：額上安上新星，手中執一支火把——他若想掙脫，火把便會吞了他。於是他永遠是索翁多瓦，那個渴念著從不認得他的星辰的獵人。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The Star Woman of the Iroquois, who precedes the sun in the east sky, is the morning star of the paleface.

passages.text: He was a mighty hunter, the So-son-do-wah! The sun glanced at the forest as it beamed upon the earth with its morning light, the forest where O-je-a-neh-doh, the Sky Elk, stood silent as a shadow as his broad antlers brushed back the branches of an oak. He had wandered far in the earth forest all the night. O-je-a-neh-doh knew not the sun, the sun does not shine on the elk fields of the sky, so far above it, whence O-je-a-neh-doh had lingered too long to return... In the honor of his hunter heart and by the law of his religion, he must give all game a chance for its life. His bent bow was waiting, his aim was sure, and his unerring arrow ready for flight when, as a warning, So-son-do-wah shook a small sapling and it whirred like a partridge taking its flight. Alert, O-je-a-neh-doh lifted his head as he snuffed the air and, with a bound, sped through the tangled ways of the hazy shades as So-son-do-wah sent his swift arrows after him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 60-61; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Hour after hour the O-je-a-neh-doh ran on, hour after hour So-son-do-wah followed... The new risen moon looked down and the stars faltered forth in the red west trail of the sun, when O-je-a-neh-doh quickened his race and leaped up the white headed hills of the sky; but So-son-do-wah, still following, caught on the wing of a swift bird of the night, which hastened its flight and soared to the farthermost part of the sky where the sun wakes up for the earth; yet O-je-a-neh-doh, the Sky Elk, more fleet in his own free fields, ever eluded the dumb arrows which sighed from So-son-do-wah's bow, until day feathered the sky with its plumes of red light, when the night bird shook So-son-do-wah from its wings back to the earth. But Dawn, pitying the sky stranger, rescued him as he was falling, and carrying him to her lodge in the east sky, created him her sentinel to guard its door.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 61; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: In his travels the heart of So-son-do-wah yearned back to the earth... Once when Day had already hinted her coming, So-son-do-wah saw a beautiful maiden standing by a low river where she had gone in search of water. Swift as an arrow of light a tenderness quivered within his heart... He could not forget the river maiden, and frequently saw her face in the river mists that rose to the sky. Although a celestial prisoner and a watcher of the night, Dawn had endowed him with dominion to enter within some other life during the day when he could revisit the earth, and one spring morning, So-son-do-wah, who in his love for the maiden had determined to find her, entered the heart of a bluebird which had dipped its wings in the azure hues of the southern sky.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 61; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: With the bird, So-son-do-wah followed the course of the river, singing 'ji-nya-ah, ji-nya-ah, ji-nya-ah,' and the forests echoed... the bluebird came at her call and sat on her shoulder and nestled its head against her face as she caressed it. Under the wing of the bird the heart of So-son-do-wah throbbed quick with love, but the sun was near and he must return to the sky... In the autumn when the trees shed their leaves and the fur of the elk grows long, So-son-do-wah crept into the heart of a giant night hawk who was searching the rivers for prey. Through the mists of the night all over the land, he called 'gwa-diis, gwa-diis' till near the sunrise, when he found the beautiful maiden sleeping on the bank. 'She is here!' whispered So-son-do-wah from the heart of the hawk as it swooped down and, lifting her to its broad wings, bore her to the skies... Dawn, who was standing by the door of her lodge, reproved So-son-do-wah for remaining so long on the earth, and transformed the maiden into a star. As punishment to So-son-do-wah for deserting his watch of her door, she invoked the aid of her warrior attendants who seized him and bound his arms. On his forehead they placed the new star, and in her hand a flaming torch, and should he attempt to release himself, the torch will consume him. And thus he remains So-son-do-wah, the human hunter, who yet yearns for the star which has never known him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 62-63; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Onatah, Spirit of the Corn, and Ga-gaah the Crow
title.zh: 玉米女神奧娜塔與烏鴉加加

region.en: The corn fields of the Seneca (symbolic pin in the Genesee valley)
region.zh: 塞內卡的玉米田（象徵性定位於傑納西河谷）

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Onatah and the Ga-gaah, Spirit of the Corn, and the Crow'

summary.en: Among the birds which came from the sun land, Ga-gaah carried in his ear a grain of corn which Hah-gweh-di-yu planted above the body of his Mother (the earth), and it became the first grain, the 'life' of the red man. By this birthright, Ga-gaah, claiming his share, hovers above the fields, guarding the young roots from the foes which infest them. Onatah, Spirit of the Corn and patroness of the fields, brings the planting season to the earth; at one time she had two companions, the spirits of the bean and the squash - the three sister plant spirits, the De-o-ha-ko, were never separated, each clothed in the plant which she guarded. One day when Onatah had wandered astray in search of the lost dews, Hah-gweh-da-et-gah, capturing her, sent one of his monsters to blight her fields, and the Spirits of the Squash and the Bean fled before the death winds which pursued them. Hah-gweh-da-et-gah imprisoned Onatah in his darkness under the earth, where she languished, lamenting her lost fields; when a searching sun ray discovered her and guided her back to her lands. Bewailing the desolation of the blight, and mourning the desertion of her sister spirits, Onatah made a vow to the Sun that she would never leave her fields again; and now she holds her vigils alone, separated from her sister plants. When Onatah brings the planting season, her crow flocks know, and the birds whirl and call in the sky; when invoking the aid of the sun, she scatters her first corn over her broad lands, the birds flutter down and hunt the foes that follow the roots in the earth.
summary.zh: 自日之邦而來的群鳥中，烏鴉加加耳中藏著一粒玉米；善靈把它種在大母親（大地）的身軀之上，便成了第一粒穀——紅人的「生命」。憑這份天賜，加加自認有份，盤旋田上，為嫩根驅除害敵。玉米女神奧娜塔——田野的守護者——把播種之季帶到人間；從前她有兩位同伴，豆靈與瓜靈：三姐妹植物精靈「德奧哈科」從不分離，各穿其所守的植物為衣。一日奧娜塔為尋遺露而迷途，惡靈哈格威達特加捕獲了她，遣怪物毀其田疇；瓜靈與豆靈被死亡之風追逐而逃散。惡靈把她囚於地下黑暗，她在其中憔悴，哭悼失落的田園；一縷尋覓的日光發現了她，引她回到自己的土地。哀荒蕪、慟離散，奧娜塔向太陽立誓永不離田——如今她獨自守夜，與姐妹精靈分離。播種季至，她的鴉群便知，在天空盤旋啼喚；她向太陽求援、把頭一把玉米撒向大地時，群鳥撲落，為她獵除纏根的禍敵。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The three sisters (Dio-he'-ko, 'our sustenance') are saluted in the green corn thanksgiving. Parker notes the Aztec parallel Tonacayohua, She Feeds Us.

passages.text: Among the birds which came from the sun land, Ga-gaah carried in his ear a grain of corn which Hah-gweh-di-yu planted above the body of his Mother (the earth), and it became the first grain, the 'life' of the red man. By this birthright, Ga-gaah, claiming his share, hovers above the fields, guarding the young roots from the foes which infest them.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 63; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Onatah, Spirit of the Corn, and patroness of the fields, brings the planting season to the earth. Onatah, chaste in her virgin beauty - the sun touches her dusky face with the blush of the morning, and her eyes grow soft as the gleam of the stars that floats on dark streams. Her night-black hair flares to the breeze like the wind-driven cloud that unveils the sun. As she walks the air draped in her maize, its blossoms plume to the sun, and its fringing tassels play with the rustling leaves in whispering promises to the waiting fields... At one time, Onatah had two companions, the spirits of the bean and the squash. In the olden time, when the bean, corn and squash were planted in one hill, these three sister plant spirits, the De-o-ha-ko were never separated. Each was clothed in the plant which she guarded.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 63-64; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: One day when Onatah had wandered astray in search of the lost dews, Hah-gweh-da-et-gah, capturing her, sent one of his monsters to blight her fields, and the Spirits of the Squash and the Bean fled before the death winds which pursued them. Hah-gweh-da-et-gah imprisoned Onatah in his darkness under the earth, where she languished, lamenting her lost fields; when a searching sun ray discovered her and guided her back to her lands. Bewailing the desolation of the blight, and mourning the desertion of her sister spirits of the bean and the squash, Onatah made a vow to the Sun that she would never leave her fields again; and now she holds her vigils alone, separated from her sister plants.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 64; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: When Onatah brings the planting season, her crow flocks know, and the birds whirl and call in the sky. When invoking the aid of the sun, Onatah scatters her first corn over her broad lands, the birds flutter down and hunt the foes that follow the roots in the earth. When the maize stalks bend low, Onatah is folding the husks to the pearly grains that the dews will nourish in their screening shade as they fringe to the sun. When the tassels plume, Onatah is crowning the maize with her triumph sign and the rustling leaves spear to the harvest breeze. The custom of 'blessing the fields' is still continued among some of the Iroquois. When the leaf of the dogwood is 'the size of a squirrel's ear,' the planting season has come. Before the dawn of the first day of the planting, a virgin girl is sent to the fields, where she scatters a few grains of corn to the earth as she invokes the assistance of the Spirit of the Corn for the harvest.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 64-66; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Gus-tah-ote, the Spirit of the Rock: A Lesson in Contentment
title.zh: 石靈古斯塔奧特：知足之課

region.en: The strong rock overhanging the valley since the world's beginning
region.zh: 開天以來俯臨山谷的巨岩

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Gus-tah-ote, Spirit of the Rock'

summary.en: Since the beginning of the earth, when the Sky Woman descended to the back of the Turtle, the strong rock had overhung the valley, and since that beginning, Gus-tah-ote, the Spirit, had been imprisoned within its silent majesty. By the law of transmigration he was offered his choice of change - to the river, or sea, or land or forest or sky. 'The majestic river flows free through its broad lands... I will try.' Down the valleys he sped, and the rhyming brooks echoed back his free song of joy; through rocky gorges he tossed the foaming waves to the sky - until a loud moaning thing encircled him with its broad arms, a mountain of water ridged high above him, and Gus-tah-ote was swept down into the gulf of a great sea. But the Rescuer reached down in the sea and caught him still breathing and returned him to the hoary old rock. He tried the sky: he plumed his wings and flew high - until a shivery wind pushed against him and tore him to fragments as it whirled him over and over in the shoreless sky; bit by bit his feathers divided, and he fell down through the labyrinthed cloud fleet to the earth. Then to the land: all through its plains of plenty and forests of fulness he traveled, yet neither a bird nor a beast nor a human was he, and no life would share with him. 'Return to your rock where you can defy all the earth... old age, who hunts for his victims all over the earth, can not wrinkle you; death can not pain nor claim you; unyielding and stanch, you will outlive all the land, the seas and the skies!' And Gus-tah-ote, the Rock Spirit, dwells there content as overhanging the valley he watches and guards.
summary.zh: 自天女降於龜背的開闢之初，那塊堅岩便俯臨山谷；石靈古斯塔奧特被囚於其沉默的威嚴之中。依轉生之律，他得選一個新的居所——河、海、大地、森林或天空。他跳入大河：順谷飛奔，溪泉應和他的歡歌；穿峽越灘，把浪花拋上天空——直到一個低吼的龐然大物張臂攏住他，水山壓頂，把他卷入大海的深淵。施救者下海把他活捉送回蒼老的岩石。他又試天空：振翅高飛——狂風撕裂他的羽翼，在無涯的天空裡把他翻卷成碎片，片片墜回大地。再試大地：他走遍豐饒的平原與茂密的森林，卻既非鳥也非獸也非人，無一生命肯容他。「回到你的岩石去吧。在那裡你可以傲視整個大地：水淹不沒你，風暴擊不倒你，烈日曬不焦你，歲月刻不皺你，死亡奈你不得；堅毅不拔，你將比大地、海洋與天空都活得長久！」於是石靈古斯塔奧特安居其上，俯臨山谷，守望如初。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. Parker: this myth suggests the life lesson of the red man - contentment.

passages.text: Since the beginning of the earth, when the Sky Woman descended to the back of the Turtle, the strong rock had overhung the valley, and since that beginning, Gus-tah-ote, the Spirit, had been imprisoned within its silent majesty. Gus-tah-ote had seen all the creations of earth grow and set themselves in place. He had seen each spirit of the animals assigned to its duty and power and had waited with observing patience till, by the law of transmigration, he too had been proffered his choice of change, whether to the river, or sea, or land or forest or sky. He could enter them, and whichever he might choose as his future abode, should be his. 'The majestic river flows free through its broad lands; I have looked down upon it for ages. There, no one would dispute my possessions,' thought Gus-tah-ote. 'I will try.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 66-67; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: As he emerged from the rock, he trod his new way bold and fearlessly strong and slipped into the river. Down the valleys sped he, and the rhyming brooks echoed back his free song of joy. Through rocky gorges he tossed the foaming waves to the sky, and they came back to him rainbowed with sunbeams. He wound around towering mountains and they poured their peaks and wrapped him in their shadows. Down a steep fall he leaped, and exulted in rapids' gladness as he tangled the waves into combating rivals... On and on, restlessly drifting, the ambitious river grew broader till no more Gus-tah-ote saw its green borders... when a loud moaning thing encircled him with its broad arms, a mountain of water ridged high above him, and Gus-tah-ote was swept down into the gulf of a great sea. But the Rescuer, who had proffered him choice of the element in which he might dwell, reached down in the sea and caught him still breathing and returned him to the hoary old rock.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 67-68; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The breath of the day was soft and as gentle as sunlight on a wild blooming flower when Gus-tah-ote tried his wings. He plumed them and fitted and fluttered them, and widened them broad to the air, and with a sneer at the bound down old rock he flew high to the sky... In his new found liberty, Gus-tah-ote flew higher, and when he looked down, the lands and the mountains and forests and rivers were far beneath him as he entered the mist land of clouds. And the air grew chill, and a something rushed past him, wounding his wings which dropped helplessly down... Bit by bit his feathers divided, and his weight growing unwieldy as he tossed near to death, Gus-tah-ote fell down through the labyrinthed cloud fleet, down through the endless free way to the earth! Senseless, unknowing, he fell, and was prostrate to his death when the Rescuer came and led him back to the rock within the valley.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 67-68; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: All through its plains of plenty and its forests of fulness he traveled, yet neither a bird nor a beast nor a human was he, and he grew lonely and strange in the new land life... no place offered shelter, no life would share with him. Thus was he despairing when the voice of the Rescuer whispered, 'Return to your rock where you can defy all the earth. The waters may overflow you but they can not drown you; the tempests may strike you, they can not overthrow you; the sun may glance at you, it can not burn you... old age, who hunts for his victims all over the earth, can not wrinkle you; death can not pain nor claim you; unyielding and stanch, you will outlive all the land, the seas and the skies!' And Gus-tah-ote, the Rock Spirit, dwells there content as overhanging the valley he watches and guards. This myth suggests the life lesson of the red man - contentment.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 68-69; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
